Tie a loose overhand knot with the doubled line. Pass the hook or lure through the large loop. Moisten, pull both standing line and tag end evenly, then trim. Keep the loop open and away from sharp points while tightening. Improved Clinch knot Mono · fluorocarbon | small hooks and terminal tackle Pass the tag end through the eye and wrap it around the standing line 5–7 times. Pass the tag through the small loop beside the eye. Pass it back through the larger loop just formed. Moisten, pull the standing line to seat the coils, and trim the tag. Use fewer wraps with thicker line; check that coils lie neatly before loading. Uni knot Mono · fluorocarbon · braid | hooks, swivels, and line connections Pass the line through the eye and double back to form a loop alongside the standing line. Wrap the tag around both parallel lines and through the loop 5–7 times. Moisten and pull the tag to snug the coils together. Slide the knot down to the eye; pull the standing line firmly and trim. For joining two lines, tie a Uni knot with each line and draw the knots together. Non-slip loop knot Mono · fluorocarbon | lures that benefit from free movement Make a loose overhand knot several inches from the tag end. Pass the tag through the lure eye, then back through the overhand knot. Wrap the tag around the standing line 4–5 times. Pass the tag back through the overhand knot the same way it entered. Moisten, tighten gradually, and verify the loop stays open at the eye. Knot diagrams vary; practice with spare line and test the connection before fishing. No knots match that search. content: Black Rockfish | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search Black Rockfish Photo: Wikimedia Commons A common nearshore rockfish of Oregon's rocky reefs and kelp habitat. Rockfish includes many species; identify each fish and check current depth, season, and bag rules. How to identify Dark charcoal to black body, often lighter underneath. Spiny dorsal fin and large eye. Black rockfish are rockfish, not true bass; similar-looking species need careful identification. Where to find them Approximate locations only. Check local access and current regulations before fishing. Brookings and Port Orford: nearshore rocky habitat reached from coastal ports. Charleston / Coos Bay: access to nearshore reef areas when conditions permit. See the coastal access map for approximate port regions, not specific fishing marks. What they eat and what to use Food Where Common presentation Small fish and krill Around rocky reefs and kelp Small metal jigs, shrimp imitations, and bait rigs Crustaceans Near bottom structure Small scented plastics or legal bait When they feed Black rockfish are caught around reef structure during safe nearshore weather windows. Use only enough weight to present gear safely near the bottom. Regulations Always verify before you go. Rockfish species can have different limits. Follow current depth restrictions and descending-device rules, and avoid marine reserves and closed areas. Check current ODFW regulations . Stocking Black rockfish are wild marine fish and are not stocked. Gear basics Medium saltwater rod with a fast-action tip. Corrosion-resistant spinning or conventional reel. Small metal jigs or bait rigs with weight matched to current. Carry and know how to use a descending device where required. What they eat and what to use Food Where Common presentation Crabs, urchins, and other invertebrates Around rocky structure Crab imitations or bait rigs near bottom Small fish Near reef habitat Small jigs and soft-plastic fish imitations When they feed Fish near rocky bottom structure when seasons are open and ocean conditions are safe. Changing current can affect whether gear can be presented near bottom. Regulations Always verify before you go. Cabezon rules are species-specific; do not assume rockfish limits apply. Check current season, size, and bag rules, and avoid closed areas. Check current ODFW regulations . Stocking Cabezon are wild marine fish and are not stocked. Gear basics Medium saltwater rod and a corrosion-resistant reel. Braided line and a strong leader for reef structure. Crab imitations, small jigs, or legal bait rigs. title: Fishing Line | Southern Oregon Angler Guide
description: Learn how monofilament, fluorocarbon, braided, and fly lines work and which fish and setups they suit.
content: Fishing Line | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search ← All gear Fishing Line Line connects you to the hook or lure. Its breaking strength, stretch, visibility, and abrasion resistance all affect casting and fish control. Line types Monofilament Stretchy, easy to knot, buoyant, and affordable. A forgiving choice for beginners, bait rigs, and treble-hook lures. Typical use: 4–8 lb for stocked trout and panfish; 8–12 lb for many bass setups. Adjust to conditions and the rod rating. Fluorocarbon Low-stretch and abrasion-resistant, and often used as a leader. It sinks more readily than mono and can be harder to knot. Typical use: light leaders for clear water and trout; heavier leaders around rocks or bass cover. Braided line Thin for its strength, with little stretch and high sensitivity. It can cut into itself on a spool and may be more visible, so anglers often add a mono or fluorocarbon leader. Typical use: bass around weeds, long casts, or situations needing sensitivity. Set the drag carefully because braid has little stretch. Fly line Thick, weighted line that loads the fly rod and carries an unweighted fly. Match the line weight and taper to the fly rod; backing sits beneath the fly line. Typical use: weight-forward floating line is a versatile starting point for many trout situations; sinking lines suit deeper presentations. Choosing line strength “Pound test” is the approximate force the line can handle under specified conditions; knots, abrasion, and wear reduce it. Start with the rod and reel’s printed line range, then consider fish size, current, cover, and lure weight. Re-tie damaged or frayed line. Line-strength suggestions are broad examples, not guarantees. Oregon waters can have special rules for line, hooks, bait, or fishing methods; check the current regulations for your exact location. title: Fishing Lures and Flies | Southern Oregon Angler Guide
description: Learn what spinners, spoons, crankbaits, soft plastics, jigs, and flies do and which Southern Oregon fish they can target.
content: Fishing Lures and Flies | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search ← All gear Lures & Flies Lures imitate prey, flash or vibrate to attract attention, or trigger a reaction strike. Choose a size and weight your rod can cast, and retrieve it at a depth and speed that fit the water. Common choices Spinners A rotating blade sends flash and vibration through the water. Cast upstream or across current and retrieve steadily. Good for: trout, steelhead, and some bass. Small spinners suit trout; larger sizes may suit bigger fish where allowed. Spoons Curved metal wobbles or flashes on retrieve. Cast them or troll them; vary speed to find a productive action. Good for: trout, kokanee, salmon, and steelhead, with size and presentation adjusted for the water. Crankbaits and hard baits Hard-bodied lures wobble, dive, or float. Their diving bill and retrieve control how deep they run. Good for: bass, trout, and other predatory fish. Match their running depth to water depth and cover. Jigs and soft plastics A weighted jig head carries a hook; soft-plastic bodies add shape and movement. Fish them on bottom, through cover, or with a swimming retrieve. Good for: bass, crappie, trout, and other species depending on size, color, and presentation. Flies Dry flies float, nymphs imitate underwater insects, and streamers imitate small fish or leeches. Fly fishing uses weighted fly line to cast these light patterns. Good for: trout and steelhead. Choose patterns that match local insects, baitfish, and water conditions. Some waters restrict bait, hooks, or lure types. Confirm the rules for the specific water before fishing. description: Compare spinning reel sizes from 1000 to 6000, baitcasters, and fly reels by use and target fish.
content: Fishing Reels | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search ← All gear Fishing Reels A reel stores line, helps retrieve it, and uses drag to let a hooked fish pull line under controlled pressure. Choose the reel type first, then size it to your rod, line, lure, and target. 1. Spinning reels: size 1000–6000 How they work The spool stays still while a rotating bail winds line onto it. They are beginner-friendly and cast light lures well. The size numbers are approximate and vary by manufacturer. Size Typical match Examples 1000–2000 Ultralight/light rod and light line Panfish, small trout, small streams and ponds 2500–3000 Light/medium all-around freshwater setup Trout, bass, kokanee, and smaller steelhead setups 4000–5000 More line capacity and drag for larger fish or current Steelhead, salmon, larger bass, and river fishing 6000 Larger/heavier setup; confirm rod balance and line capacity Large salmon, strong current, or heavier presentations A size number is not a universal measurement. Check a reel’s actual line capacity and drag, and balance it with the rod instead of choosing by number alone. 2. Baitcasting reels Low-profile and round baitcasters The spool rotates as line leaves it, giving accurate casts and direct control with medium to heavy lures. Magnetic or centrifugal brakes help control spool speed; the thumb controls it during a cast. Good for: largemouth and smallmouth bass around cover, heavier lures, and some salmon setups. Choose a reel by rod pairing, line capacity, and drag, not spinning-reel size numbers. Browse placeholder reels → 3. Fly reels Match the reel to fly-rod weight Fly reels hold backing and fly line, retrieve line, and provide drag. Choose a reel labeled for the same line weight as the rod and fly line (for example, a 5-weight reel for a 5-weight outfit). A large arbor retrieves line faster and reduces line memory. Good for: trout and steelhead when paired with a suitable fly rod, line, and backing. Fly reels are not sized with the 1000–6000 spinning scale. Reel recommendations are starting points. Check current ODFW regulations and size gear for the water and fish.

title: Fishing Rods | Southern Oregon Angler Guide
description: Compare spinning, casting, and fly rods, and learn how rod length, power, and action match Southern Oregon fish.
content: Fishing Rods | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search ← All gear Fishing Rods A rod casts the lure or bait, helps control the line, and cushions a fish’s runs. Choose its style to match the reel, then match length, power, and action to your target and fishing spot. Rod styles Spinning rods Designed for spinning reels mounted below the rod. Easy to learn and versatile with light lures, bait, and floats. Good for: stocked trout, panfish, bass, and general bank or boat fishing. Casting rods Designed for baitcasting reels mounted above the rod. Their trigger grip and guides suit heavier lures and accurate casts. Good for: bass fishing around weeds or cover, and heavier lures. They take practice to cast without line overruns. Fly rods Built to cast weighted fly line, which carries a lightweight fly. Rod weight (such as 3-weight or 5-weight) should match the fly line and reel. Good for: trout and steelhead with flies. A 3–5 weight is common for trout; larger fish and heavier flies call for a stronger setup. Length, power, and action Rod choice What it means Common use 5–6 ft, ultralight/light Short, light rod for small lures and delicate presentations. Bluegill, crappie, stocked trout on small ponds or tight streams. 6–7 ft, light/medium Versatile cast distance and control; handles many light-to-medium lures. Trout, kokanee, bass, and general freshwater fishing. 7–9 ft, medium/medium-heavy Longer casts and more leverage; power for current or larger lures. Steelhead, salmon, bass in cover, and larger rivers. Fast action Bends mostly near the tip for quick response and hook-setting. Jigs, soft plastics, and many all-purpose setups. Moderate action Bends farther down the blank, helping cast and keep treble-hook lures pinned. Crankbaits, spoons, and moving lures. Match the rod’s printed line and lure ratings. Rod lengths and powers are not standardized across brands, so use the ratings printed on the rod as your guide. Browse placeholder rods → Always check current ODFW fishing regulations .

title: Fishing Tackle | Southern Oregon Angler Guide
description: A beginner guide to hooks, bobbers, sinkers, swivels, leaders, and the jobs they do in a fishing rig.
content: Fishing Tackle | Southern Oregon Angler Guide Menu Angler Guide Fish Waters Gear Setup Builder Trip Planning Fishing Calendar Fishing Log Newsletter Regulations Search the whole site Search ← All gear Terminal Tackle Terminal tackle is the small hardware at the business end of your line. Each piece changes how bait or a lure is presented. What each piece does Hooks Hold bait or a lure and connect the fish to the line. Hook size should match the bait and target fish; a bigger hook is not automatically better. Remove or replace bent and rusty hooks. Used for: bait fishing, soft plastics, and fly or lure rigs. Follow water-specific barbless or hook restrictions. Browse placeholder tackle → Bobbers / floats Keep bait suspended at a set depth and show a bite. Adjust the depth so bait sits near where fish are feeding without dragging along the bottom. Used for: trout, panfish, and river presentations such as a float-and-jig setup. Weights and sinkers Help cast and take bait or a lure down to depth. Use only enough weight to reach the intended zone; current and depth determine how much is needed. Used for: bottom rigs, drift fishing, and some bait presentations. Check for local restrictions on sinker materials. Swivels and snaps A swivel can reduce line twist; a snap makes changing lures easier. Extra hardware can affect a lure’s action, so use the smallest practical size. Used for: spinning lures, spoons, and rigs that tend to twist line. Leaders A short section between main line and hook or lure. Leaders can add abrasion resistance, change visibility, or make a fly setup easier to rig. Used for: trout in clear water, bass around cover, and fly fishing. Choose material and strength to suit the fish and main line. Hook and tackle rules vary by water. Check current ODFW regulations .
